abilities.text: Improves the unit's ability to defend at the cost of their mobility.

abilities.text: Charges are more effective for an extended time.

attributes.text: This unit can hide in forests until enemy units get too close.

attributes.text: This unit is immune to the fear effects of scary units.

short: Schola - one of the features of the Later Roman military organization was the creation of new guard units - Scholae Palatinae, which replaced the Praetorian Guard. The latter was finally dissolved by Constantine after his victory over Maxentius. T. Mommsen believed that the scholas were a creation of Constantine. R. Frank attributed this event to the period after 312 AD, after the disbanding of the Praetorian cohorts. In the laws from the Codex Theodosius, it is reported that Constantine granted the right annona civica to two scholae - schola scutariorum and schola clibanariorum, they are considered to be the first scholas. The armament of the scholae differed from the rest of the army. Describing the battle of Argentaria, Ammianus Marcellinus writes that «the shining gold and colorful armor of the imperial guard bent under the frequent blows of throwing projectiles». Despite their military status, the scholae were never under the command of the magister militum and were formally at the disposal of the magister officiorum. Each schola was commanded by a tribune; the tribunes themselves were under the direct command of the Emperor. About number of scholas is judged on a fragment from «Secret History» of Procopius of Caesarea where he writes that during Justinian the imperial palace in Constantinople was guarded by 3,5 thousand scholarians from seven scholae. That is, the number of one schola was about 500 men. Scutarii derive their name from the Latin word scutum, meaning «shield» and literally translated as shield-bearers, but this name was only given to special ranked units.
history: Rome’s Empire became so large that in its later period the Emperor could not be everywhere at once. As such he appointed ‘Comites’, trusted, high-ranking military and administrative figures who ran certain parts of the Empire in his stead. ‘Comes’ – the singular - is Latin for ‘Companion’, used here in direct reference to the Companions of Alexander the Great, the most trusted lieutenants of the greatest military leader the world had yet seen (and someone all Roman Emperors aspired to be like). The Comites were the Emperor’s own inner circle, the leading officials of the Empire, wielding posts of myriad descriptions and reasonability, from the ‘Comes Britanniarum’, who was in charge of Roman Britain’s defence, to the ‘Comes Sacrae Vestis’ – master of the Emperor’s wardrobe!
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
